interview_metadata.name: Andrew Black
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) ??? Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: I was born in Cedar Rapids, Iowa, in 1955, in a pretty ordinary Midwestern family. My father worked with his hands and with plans, first in a cabinet shop and later around construction drafting, and my mother was a school secretary and library aide, so books and tools were both normal things in our house. I was the sort of boy who took apart radios, built birdhouses, and spent too much time staring at clouds when I was supposed to be mowing. I did some college at a community college and took drafting and design courses, but I never finished a four-year degree. I went into carpentry and architectural drafting because it let me think spatially and still come home with sawdust on my sleeves. I married Margaret, whom everyone calls Maggie, in my late twenties, and we raised two children while I worked remodels, custom cabinetry, and small residential design jobs. Retirement came gradually rather than all at once; my knees and hands told me to slow down, and the high desert around Payson gave me a place to turn toward painting, photography, writing, and mentoring older folks who want to tell their stories.

follow_ups.question: What do you remember most vividly from your childhood home?
follow_ups.response: The smell of coffee and pine shavings, my mother typing school notices at the kitchen table, and my father sharpening chisels in the basement on Saturday mornings.

follow_ups.question: Who were the main people shaping you when you were young?
follow_ups.response: My parents, a high school art teacher named Mr. Reynolds, and an uncle who took me fishing and taught me that patience was a form of intelligence.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: The clearest crossroads was in my early thirties. I had a chance to go full-time into an architectural office in Des Moines, which would have meant steadier pay and maybe a more professional title, or stay closer to hands-on carpentry and small projects. Maggie and I had one child then and another coming, so steady pay was tempting. But I realized I did not want to spend my whole life only revising drawings under fluorescent lights. I chose the smaller path: custom carpentry, remodeling, and design work where I could talk to clients, solve problems on site, and see the finished thing. It probably cost me money, but it preserved the part of me that needed craft, independence, and direct contact with materials.

follow_ups.question: Did Maggie have a strong opinion about that choice?
follow_ups.response: She wanted us to be practical, but she also knew I would sour if I was boxed in, so she helped me make a budget instead of pushing me one way.

follow_ups.question: What did that decision change day to day?
follow_ups.response: It meant early mornings, job-site coffee, driving a pickup full of tools, and sometimes doing estimates at the kitchen table after the children were asleep.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: It was conscious, though not dramatic. I remember sitting with a yellow legal pad and writing out numbers, then realizing the choice was also about what kind of man I wanted to become.

follow_ups.question: Did you feel certain at the time?
follow_ups.response: No, I felt responsible more than certain.

follow_ups.question: How long did it take you to decide?
follow_ups.response: A few weeks of talking, calculating, and walking around with it.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: A small-business mentor would have helped. I learned estimating, taxes, insurance, and client contracts mostly by making mistakes.

follow_ups.question: Where did you eventually get advice?
follow_ups.response: Older tradesmen, the public library, and one patient accountant who explained quarterly taxes without making me feel foolish.

follow_ups.question: Would you mentor someone now in that position?
follow_ups.response: Yes, and I would start with pricing their time honestly.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: I am married to Maggie Black, and we have been married a little over forty years. She is retired from library work, which suited her because she has always been orderly, curious, and quietly formidable. We have two adult children: Laura lives in Flagstaff and works in health care, and David lives down in Mesa and teaches high school science. We have four grandchildren, and they are old enough now that visits involve real conversations, not just spilled juice and cartoons. Maggie is my daily companion, but she and I also give each other room; she gardens and reads mysteries, while I might be out before dawn photographing the Mogollon Rim. Family matters to me most through ordinary contact: Sunday calls, birthdays remembered, grandchildren visiting in the summer, and the occasional argument about whether I should still climb ladders.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see your children and grandchildren?
follow_ups.response: Laura comes down every month or two, David's family a little less often, and we do video calls with the grandchildren most Sunday evenings.

follow_ups.question: What do you and Maggie usually do together?
follow_ups.response: We share breakfast, take short walks, watch a ballgame now and then, and go to community concerts or art openings when Payson has them.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: I have a younger sister, Elaine, still in Iowa. We talk by phone every couple of weeks and keep the old family stories alive.

follow_ups.question: Are you close emotionally?
follow_ups.response: Yes, in a Midwestern way: not flowery, but dependable.

follow_ups.question: Do you visit her?
follow_ups.response: Usually once a year if travel and health cooperate.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: My circle is not large, but it is steady. I have hiking friends through the Desert Peaks Hiking Association, a chess group at the senior center, and a small group of artists who meet twice a month to critique work and drink mediocre coffee. My closest friend here is Ron Castillo, a retired electrician who knows birds better than anyone I have met. There is also Judith, who co-facilitates writing workshops with me; she is sharp and kind and keeps me from wandering too far into abstraction.

follow_ups.question: How often do you spend time with friends?
follow_ups.response: Two or three times a week in some form, between hiking, chess, workshops, and coffee after yoga.

follow_ups.question: What do you usually talk about with them?
follow_ups.response: Bird sightings, grandchildren, health annoyances, local politics, books, and whether the Diamondbacks bullpen is going to hold.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: We live in Payson, Arizona, in a quiet neighborhood with junipers, ponderosa pines, and enough open sky to make me happy. It is not fancy, but most people keep up their places and wave from driveways. You hear dogs, pickup trucks, and mourning doves more than traffic. The town has a slower pace than Phoenix, and that suits us. I like being close to trails, the Rim, the library, the senior center, and a grocery store that still feels manageable.

follow_ups.question: What is your usual route around the neighborhood?
follow_ups.response: I walk a loop of about a mile and a half, usually before 8 a.m., past a wash where I sometimes see quail.

follow_ups.question: Do you know your neighbors well?
follow_ups.response: A few well enough to exchange garden produce, check mail, and notice if someone's porch light has been on too long.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: I feel generally safe. We lock doors, of course, but I do not walk around worried.

follow_ups.question: Has anything happened nearby that made you uneasy?
follow_ups.response: Mostly minor property thefts from unlocked vehicles, nothing that changed how we live.

follow_ups.question: Do you feel safe walking early in the morning?
follow_ups.response: Yes, though I carry a small light and pay attention to footing and wildlife more than people.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: The beauty and quiet are the upsides. The harder parts are summer fire danger, limited specialty medical care, and the fact that you drive farther for certain things.

follow_ups.question: What do you miss from bigger towns?
follow_ups.response: A wider choice of museums, music, and restaurants.

follow_ups.question: What would be hardest to give up here?
follow_ups.response: The morning light on the Rim and the sense that people still recognize one another.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: Right now it is just Maggie and me in the house. We have a small three-bedroom place, though one bedroom is really my painting and photo-editing room now. No one is staying with us temporarily at the moment. The house runs on quiet routines: Maggie in the garden, me in the garage shop or at my desk, and both of us trying not to leave reading glasses in ridiculous places.

follow_ups.question: Do you share household tasks?
follow_ups.response: Yes, Maggie handles more of the bills and garden planning, and I cook several nights, do repairs, and manage the heavier errands.

follow_ups.question: Which rooms do you use the most?
follow_ups.response: The kitchen, my converted studio room, the garage workshop, and the back patio when the weather behaves.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: Everyone is permanent; it is just Maggie and me.

follow_ups.question: No one staying short term right now?
follow_ups.response: No, not right now.

follow_ups.question: Does that change seasonally?
follow_ups.response: Only when grandchildren visit for a few days.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: Our grandchildren sometimes stay during summer breaks or a long weekend.

follow_ups.question: Where do they sleep?
follow_ups.response: In the guest room and sometimes on the old foldout couch.

follow_ups.question: How long do visits usually last?
follow_ups.response: Usually two to five nights.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No, nobody usually lives here besides us.

follow_ups.question: No one away at school?
follow_ups.response: No.

follow_ups.question: No one in care or hospital?
follow_ups.response: No, thankfully.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: I am usually up by 5:30, earlier if the sky is clear and I want to photograph stars before dawn. Mondays and Thursdays often include low-impact yoga at the senior center. Tuesdays I may work on paintings or photo edits, and Wednesday afternoons I help with a writing workshop. Fridays are errands, library, and sometimes chess. Weekends depend on family or the hiking association; if there is a bird walk, I am likely to be there with binoculars and a thermos of dark coffee.

follow_ups.question: What does a normal morning look like?
follow_ups.response: Coffee, a notebook, weather check, maybe a short walk, then either studio time or a planned outing by 8:30.

follow_ups.question: When do you usually wind down?
follow_ups.response: After dinner I read, listen to piano music, or sort photographs, and I am usually in bed around 10.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: I am retired and not in the workforce now. I used to work as a carpenter, cabinetmaker, and occasional architectural drafter for residential remodels and custom projects. These days I do unpaid or very small-stipend community work: creative writing workshops, art mentoring, and helping older adults learn basic photo editing. I treat those commitments seriously, but they are not jobs in the old sense.

follow_ups.question: How many hours do you spend volunteering or mentoring?
follow_ups.response: Usually six to ten hours a week, more if a workshop is coming up.

follow_ups.question: Do you still take paid carpentry work?
follow_ups.response: No, I might fix a neighbor's loose shelf, but I do not take paid jobs anymore.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: I keep up the house repairs, because an old carpenter has no excuse for a loose railing. I water the garden when Maggie asks, maintain our car and RV records, and manage my photography equipment. I also call my sister regularly and try to write at least three mornings a week. There is a meditation practice too, usually ten minutes, nothing dramatic.

follow_ups.question: What responsibilities do you never skip?
follow_ups.response: Medication, checking in with Maggie about the day, and locking up the garage shop.

follow_ups.question: What do you write in the mornings?
follow_ups.response: Memoir sketches, poems, and small essays about perception, memory, and landscape.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: The main change is that I have been spending more time indoors during smoky or very hot days. I used to push through more, but now I adjust. I also added a weekly balance class after a friend took a bad fall on a trail. Maggie and I have become more deliberate about appointments and rest days, which is one of those unglamorous truths of being seventy.

follow_ups.question: When did you add the balance class?
follow_ups.response: About six months ago, after Ron's fall on loose gravel.

follow_ups.question: Has it changed your hiking?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I use trekking poles more and choose routes with better footing.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: My children are adults now, so I am far removed from school pickup lines. When they were young, mornings were lunches, backpacks, and me leaving for job sites by seven. Laura played clarinet and later volunteered at the hospital, and David did soccer and science club. Now I mostly hear about my grandchildren's schedules: robotics, soccer, choir, and too much homework by my estimation.

follow_ups.question: Do you help with grandchildren's school routines?
follow_ups.response: Only from a distance, mostly encouragement, occasional homework conversations, and summer museum trips.

follow_ups.question: What do you like doing with them educationally?
follow_ups.response: Night-sky photography, temple and museum visits, and showing them how to notice details.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: My personal experiences have been limited and mostly ordinary. I have had a couple of traffic stops over the decades, one for speeding years ago and one warning for a taillight. In Payson I see police at community events and on the roads, but I have not had serious direct contact. I am aware that my experience as an older white man is not the same as everyone's.

follow_ups.question: How were you treated during those stops?
follow_ups.response: Politely, and I was polite back.

follow_ups.question: Do you know local officers personally?
follow_ups.response: Only in passing from town events and neighborhood safety meetings.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: A burglary report from a job site in the 1990s stands out. Tools were stolen, and the police took a report, but nothing came of it.

follow_ups.question: Did that affect your work habits?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I became meticulous about locking tool trailers and marking equipment.

follow_ups.question: Did you feel helped?
follow_ups.response: I felt heard, but not exactly helped in recovering anything.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: I have never been arrested, and no immediate family member has either. I have known a few tradesmen over the years who had DUI arrests, but not close family.

follow_ups.question: Did those experiences affect how you thought about drinking and driving?
follow_ups.response: Very much; I have always been firm about not mixing the two.

follow_ups.question: Were those close friends?
follow_ups.response: Work acquaintances more than close friends.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I vote regularly, including local elections. Maggie and I both believe that school boards, county supervisors, and water issues matter as much as the big national races. I usually read the voter pamphlet, mark it up, and mail my ballot early. I have missed maybe one local election in the last decade, and that bothered me.

follow_ups.question: How do you decide on local candidates?
follow_ups.response: I look at experience, temperament, land and water positions, and whether they seem interested in governing rather than performing.

follow_ups.question: Do you discuss your vote with Maggie?
follow_ups.response: Yes, though we do not always vote exactly the same.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I would call myself an Independent who leans Democratic, though I am not a party loyalist by temperament. I am fairly conservation-minded, both environmentally and culturally, in the sense that I think communities should preserve land, libraries, craft, and public institutions. I support civil rights, voting access, public education, and sensible gun rules, but I also value local knowledge and do not think every problem is solved from Washington. I grew up around practical conservatives, and I still respect thrift and responsibility, but the national Republican Party has moved away from what I recognize. Climate, water, public lands, and democratic norms weigh heavily on me now. I distrust cruelty dressed up as policy.

follow_ups.question: What issues most often determine your vote?
follow_ups.response: Democracy, public education, conservation, health care access, and whether a candidate treats opponents like human beings.

follow_ups.question: Do you ever vote Republican?
follow_ups.response: In the past I did for local offices, but much less often in recent years.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: I have become more protective of democratic institutions than I was twenty years ago. I used to assume the basic rules were stable and that most public officials accepted them. Now I do not assume that. I have also become more attentive to water policy, fire management, and climate change because those are not abstract in Arizona. Another change is that I listen more carefully to younger people on race, gender, and economic pressure than I did when I was working full time and tired all the time.

follow_ups.question: What made democracy feel less secure to you?
follow_ups.response: The 2020 election aftermath and the language around it shook me.

follow_ups.question: Who has influenced you recently?
follow_ups.response: My children, younger workshop participants, and some careful long-form journalism.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: They have affected me somewhat to a lot, mostly by making me examine what I had been able not to see. I grew up in mostly white spaces, and it is easy in that setting to think fairness is just a matter of individual manners. Listening to Black Americans describe policing and everyday suspicion made me realize how narrow my own experience was. I would not claim to be an expert or activist, but I do not dismiss it.

follow_ups.question: Was there a particular moment that stayed with you?
follow_ups.response: The George Floyd video was hard to watch and harder to forget.

follow_ups.question: Did it change conversations in your home?
follow_ups.response: Yes, Maggie and I talked about policing, history, and what we had not been taught.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think about them as issues of dignity, accountability, and unequal vulnerability. Police have a difficult job, but that cannot be the end of the conversation. Public power needs public accountability. I also think the phrase made some people defensive before they listened to the substance. For me, the basic point is that some citizens have not been protected or respected equally.

follow_ups.question: Do you support police reform?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially better accountability, training, mental health response, and transparent review after serious incidents.

follow_ups.question: Do your friends agree?
follow_ups.response: Some do, some are skeptical, and a few do not want to talk about it.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: I think race is woven into American history more deeply than many of us were taught. In Arizona I also think about Native American history and Mexican American communities, because this land carries older stories than my own family's migration west. I try to approach it with humility. That means reading, listening, and being careful about assuming good intentions erase unequal outcomes.

follow_ups.question: Has living in Arizona changed that perspective?
follow_ups.response: Yes, because tribal nations, Spanish place names, border politics, and water rights are present in daily geography.

follow_ups.question: Do those ideas enter your art?
follow_ups.response: Carefully; I use local landscape motifs but try not to appropriate sacred imagery I do not understand.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: I have talked with family and friends, donated modestly to civil rights and voter access groups, and read more. I have not joined large protests, partly because of age and health caution.

follow_ups.question: Who do you talk with most openly?
follow_ups.response: My daughter Laura and my workshop co-facilitator Judith.

follow_ups.question: Do you raise it in workshops?
follow_ups.response: Only when relevant to a participant's writing, and then I try to hold the space respectfully.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: Maggie is thoughtful and probably more direct than I am. Laura is strongly engaged and reads a great deal about health disparities. David teaches teenagers, so he sees how these discussions affect classrooms. Some of my older friends are uncomfortable and feel accused, while others have tried to learn. The conversations are not always easy, but I would rather have clumsy honest talk than silence.

follow_ups.question: Has anyone close to you changed their mind?
follow_ups.response: One hiking friend softened after his granddaughter challenged him with more patience than I could have managed.

follow_ups.question: Do you avoid any conversations?
follow_ups.response: I avoid shouting matches, especially on Facebook.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: For seventy, I am doing fairly well. I have controlled high blood pressure, some osteoarthritis in my hands and knees, and I need reading glasses that I constantly misplace. My hearing is not what it was after years around saws. I hike, do low-impact yoga, and try to eat sensibly. I am not trying to be twenty-five; I am trying to remain steady and useful.

follow_ups.question: What medications do you take regularly?
follow_ups.response: A blood pressure medication, a statin, vitamin D, and occasional ibuprofen if my joints complain.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see a doctor?
follow_ups.response: Usually twice a year for primary care, plus eye and dental visits.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: It is easier because I like walking, cooking at home, and quiet routines. It is harder because joints stiffen, medical specialists are not always close, and Arizona heat can keep me indoors. I also have to remind myself that moderation is not surrender. The senior center helps by making exercise social enough that I show up.

follow_ups.question: What foods help you feel healthy?
follow_ups.response: Vegetables, trout, soups, sourdough in reasonable amounts, and strong coffee before noon.

follow_ups.question: What tends to throw you off?
follow_ups.response: Travel, smoke from fires, and family visits with too many desserts.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: The biggest thing was a small basal cell skin cancer removed from my left temple last year. It was caught early, but it reminded me that years of outdoor work and hiking leave a mark. I also had a flare of knee pain after a steep trail and did physical therapy for about six weeks. No broken bones, no major hospital stay. I am more religious about hats and sunscreen now.

follow_ups.question: Did the skin cancer scare you?
follow_ups.response: A little, mostly because the word cancer lands heavily even when the doctor is calm.

follow_ups.question: Did physical therapy help?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially strengthening around the knee and changing how I descend trails.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: My health does not stop me from daily responsibilities, but it does set boundaries. I no longer climb roofs, carry heavy lumber, or hike without considering distance, heat, and footing.

follow_ups.question: Does pain affect your art or writing?
follow_ups.response: Hand stiffness can shorten painting sessions, so I stretch and take breaks.

follow_ups.question: Does it affect family care?
follow_ups.response: Only in that I am less likely to chase grandchildren up a hill than I once was.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: Maggie has had some thyroid issues and a hip replacement several years ago, so we have been through periods where I was the driver, cook, and reminder system. My sister has diabetes, and I worry about her from a distance. Among friends, health is a regular topic now: falls, heart procedures, caregiving for spouses. It is part of the social weather at our age.

follow_ups.question: How did Maggie's hip recovery change the household?
follow_ups.response: For a couple of months I handled most errands, laundry, meals, and making sure she did her exercises.

follow_ups.question: Do friends support each other around health?
follow_ups.response: Yes, we drive one another to appointments sometimes and check in after procedures.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?
transcript.response: We are fortunate to have Medicare and supplemental coverage, so we have not had to forgo essential care recently. The challenge is access and distance. Some specialists require a trip to Phoenix or Flagstaff, which turns an appointment into a full-day undertaking. Dental and hearing costs are still sobering. I would not call us deprived, but I understand how quickly a medical bill can frighten a retired household.

follow_ups.question: What care is hardest to access locally?
follow_ups.response: Specialists, dermatology appointments, and certain imaging follow-ups.

follow_ups.question: Do costs ever delay care?
follow_ups.response: For dental or hearing aids, yes, we sometimes time things carefully.

transcript.question_text: Have you or your immediate family ever used alternative forms of medicine? This might include indigenous, non-western, or informal forms of care.
transcript.response: We mostly use conventional medicine, but I do yoga, meditation, and breathing exercises, and I tried acupuncture for back pain years ago. Maggie uses herbal teas, though she checks interactions because she is sensible. I respect traditional healing practices, but I do not borrow from Native practices casually or treat them like decoration. For me, alternative care means supportive habits alongside regular medical care, not replacing it.

follow_ups.question: Did acupuncture help?
follow_ups.response: It helped me relax, though I cannot say it cured the back problem.

follow_ups.question: How often do you meditate?
follow_ups.response: Most mornings for about ten minutes.

transcript.question_text: During tough times, some people tell us they cope by smoking or drinking. How about for you?
transcript.response: I do not smoke and never really did beyond foolish experiments as a teenager. I drink modestly: a beer during a ballgame or a glass of wine with dinner, maybe two or three drinks in a week. During tough times I am more likely to walk, sand a piece of wood, write, or sit quietly outside. Alcohol has never been my main coping tool.

follow_ups.question: What is your usual drink if you have one?
follow_ups.response: A local amber beer or a glass of red wine.

follow_ups.question: Has drinking ever caused problems?
follow_ups.response: No, I have kept it pretty moderate.

transcript.question_text: Other people say they cope by relying on prescriptions, pain medications, marijuana, or other substances. How about for you and can you describe your most recent experience of using them, if any?
transcript.response: I take prescribed medication for blood pressure and cholesterol, but not for coping emotionally. For pain, I use ibuprofen occasionally and try not to overdo it. I tried a CBD cream on my knee once because a friend swore by it, but I did not notice much. I do not use marijuana or other substances. The most recent pain medication was two ibuprofen after a long hike, with dinner and plenty of water.

follow_ups.question: Do you worry about medication dependence?
follow_ups.response: I am cautious because I saw people in the trades get into trouble with pain pills.

follow_ups.question: What do you do before taking pain medicine?
follow_ups.response: Stretch, rest, ice if needed, and ask whether I am being stubborn.

transcript.question_text: How are you and your family coping with, or paying for, your health care needs right now?
transcript.response: Medicare, a supplemental plan, Social Security, Maggie's small pension, and retirement savings cover our needs. We budget for premiums, prescriptions, dental work, and travel to appointments. I keep a folder with medical bills because otherwise paper multiplies like rabbits, though I suppose I should not blame the paper. We are managing, but we are careful.

follow_ups.question: Who handles the paperwork?
follow_ups.response: Maggie handles most bills, and I keep appointment notes and receipts.

follow_ups.question: What health expense worries you most?
follow_ups.response: Long-term care, because that can overwhelm even careful planning.

transcript.question_text: Some people are excited about medical vaccination, and others, not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: I am pro-vaccination. I get flu shots, COVID boosters when recommended, shingles, pneumonia, the routine ones for someone my age.

follow_ups.question: Did you have concerns about COVID vaccines?
follow_ups.response: I watched the evidence, but I trusted the medical consensus and got vaccinated.

follow_ups.question: Does Maggie feel the same?
follow_ups.response: Yes, she is even more prompt about scheduling them.

transcript.question_text: What are your trusted sources of information about the vaccine?
transcript.response: My primary care doctor is first. I also look at CDC guidance, Mayo Clinic materials, and occasionally local public health updates. transcript.question_text: What was her job? What kind of work did she do? What were her most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: She was a school secretary and later helped in the school library. She typed notices, answered phones, kept attendance records, helped teachers, and guided children toward books. Her most important duty was keeping the school office humane and orderly.

follow_ups.question: Did students know her well?
follow_ups.response: Yes, many came to her when they needed help finding something or calming down.

follow_ups.question: Did she bring work home?
follow_ups.response: Mostly stories, not paperwork.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did she work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where she worked?
transcript.response: She worked for a public elementary school. It was not a business in the manufacturing sense; it educated children, kept records, supported teachers, and served families in the neighborhood.

follow_ups.question: Was it close to home?
follow_ups.response: Yes, close enough that school life and neighborhood life overlapped.

follow_ups.question: Did you visit her workplace?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes, especially after school.

transcript.question_text: Did your dad work for pay for at least a year while you were growing up?
transcript.response: Yes, he worked for pay throughout my childhood.

follow_ups.question: Was he the main earner?
follow_ups.response: Yes, for most of my childhood.

follow_ups.question: Did he work long hours?
follow_ups.response: Often, especially when construction schedules were tight.

transcript.question_text: What was his job? What kind of work did he do? What were his most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: He worked as a cabinetmaker and later as a shop foreman with drafting responsibilities. He measured, cut, assembled, supervised younger workers, read plans, and made sure finished work was square and solid. His most important duties were accuracy, safety, and keeping promises to customers.

follow_ups.question: Did he teach you carpentry?
follow_ups.response: Yes, beginning with sweeping floors and sharpening tools.

follow_ups.question: What did you learn from him besides craft?
follow_ups.response: To be calm under pressure and not hide mistakes.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did he work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where he worked?
transcript.response: He worked for a small millwork and cabinet shop connected to residential and commercial construction. They made cabinets, trim, counters, built-ins, and custom wood pieces for homes, schools, and offices.

follow_ups.question: Was it a large company?
follow_ups.response: No, a small local business.

follow_ups.question: Did you ever work there?
follow_ups.response: I helped in small ways as a teenager and later did similar work myself.

transcript.question_text: We all have hopes about what our future will look like. Imagine yourself a few years from now. Maybe you want your life to be the same in some ways as it is now. Maybe you want it to be different in some ways. What do you hope for?
transcript.response: I hope Maggie and I remain healthy enough to stay in our home, walk our neighborhood, and travel modestly. I would like to finish a memoir manuscript, not because I expect fame, but because I want to leave a truthful account for my family. I hope to expand the community workshops a little, especially around digital photography and writing from memory. I would like to take one more serious night-sky trip, maybe to Utah or the Atacama if health and money allow. Mostly I hope to remain curious and useful, and not become so cautious that wonder disappears.

follow_ups.question: What would finishing the memoir mean to you?
follow_ups.response: It would gather the fragments of work, family, landscape, and aging into something my grandchildren could hold.

follow_ups.question: What do you hope stays exactly the same?
follow_ups.response: Morning coffee with Maggie and access to open sky.

transcript.question_text: What do you value the most in your life?
transcript.response: I value fidelity, curiosity, and care. By fidelity I mean showing up for the people and places that have entrusted themselves to you: spouse, children, friends, community, land. Curiosity keeps the world from becoming small. Care is what turns skill into service, whether that is building a cabinet, teaching someone to write a memory, or listening when a friend is frightened.

follow_ups.question: What value do you hope your grandchildren learn from you?
follow_ups.response: Attention: to people, to craft, to history, and to the natural world.

follow_ups.question: What makes a good life in your view?
follow_ups.response: Useful work, honest love, enough quiet to think, and enough courage to keep learning.
